In collaboration with the Girls Action Foundation, La Converse is proud to present the podcast UNBOXED. The project is hosted in English by four students: Charlie, Maiya, Rena and Gheerti. We are delighted to share this wonderful project, which raises many crucial questions about identity, stereotypes and our relationship to community. As part of a joint effort to serve English-speaking QTBIPOC women in Montréal, we worked with some remarkable people to ensure the project's success. For everything related to sound recording, editing and design, we worked with Emmanuelle from La Zone Podcast. Emmanuelle described the project as an “enriching experience,” and we completely agree with her. It was also stimulating for us at La Converse, because we were able to make room for the stories of these brilliant, creative young minds. Speaking of brilliant minds, we warmly thank Allison from the Girls Action Foundation for finding the perfect candidates for a project like this. The effort and care she showed contributed extraordinarily to the project's success.
<strong>Est-ce qu'une étiquette est quel: Is a label something to embrace? Or something to ignore? Even a tool for empowerment?
Dans le cadre du premier projet de balad: As part of École Converse's first podcast project, we are happy to help Charlie, Maiya, Rena and Gheerti structure their ideas and present them in an organized, concise and intriguing way. The project begins by defining what a label is: “To label someone is to put them in a box, to categorize someone based on your own interpretations or prejudices” (Episode 1: <l1>Peeling Back the Label</l1>), and soon after, it explores what a label can be when it is self-assigned.
Adoptant approche intersectionnelle pour: Taking an intersectional approach to exploring the idea of labelling, Charlie, Maiya, Rena and Gheerti discuss and explore their own identities throughout the project, asking themselves pointed questions such as these: is a label something to embrace? Or something to ignore? Even a tool for empowerment? Over the course of the two episodes, we learn that labels are endless and can be about anything – from race and gender to mental illness, physical ability, sexual identity, nationality and profession – and that they change.
<strong>Mais qui sont ces jeunes remarqu: But who are these remarkable young people, and what labels do they use?!
S'inspirant du premier épisode du balado: Drawing on the first episode of the podcast (<l1>Peeling Back the Label</l1>), each participant initially defined themselves differently, but there were also things in common, since most of them gave themselves the label “neurodivergent.” Gheerti described herself as “Tamil, autistic, [with] she/her pronouns,” and Rena said her pronouns were “she” and described herself as a “student.” Maiya said they use any pronouns and are “part of the LGBTQ community” and “a student too.” Charlie, going last, introduced themself as “gender fluid,” using the pronouns “he, they, she and purr,” and also as an “immigrant from the United States.”
Travailler avec ces jeunes a été extrême: Working with these young people was extremely rewarding, because we were able to shine a light on subjects that are especially important and relevant in both the public and private spheres. “Working with Charlie, Maiya, Rena and Gheerti was fun and inspiring. We really enjoyed listening to them and helping them express their concerns about today's society and turn them into the podcast UNBOXED, an informed conversation about the labels that are assigned to us and the effects they have on us,” says our editor-in-chief, Lela Savić.
Nous avons appris à nous servir de certa: We learned to use certain tools to better understand that labels are created, consciously and unconsciously, and assigned to different groups within our society, carrying both negative and positive connotations: “According to research, people who are labelled negatively are more likely to act in deviant ways. Positive labelling acts as positive reinforcement, while negative labels act as negative reinforcement” (Episode 2: Labels Stick). We were also able to connect with the podcast on a very introspective level, asking ourselves which labels we accept and defend or, on the contrary, reject, and how these labels represent us and our multifaceted identities. As Gheerti observes in Episode 1: Peeling Back the Label, “[r]epresenting comes with a lot of pressure though… and I think that's where you [can] kind of get boxed in; they think you're a representative of all Tamil people, and everyone is different.” Which part of UNBOXED did you enjoy the most? What labels do you use to define yourself, if any? Listen to the podcast UNBOXED today to discover hidden gems, and let us know your favourite part of the project!
